title: CJI Surya Kant Threatens to Intervene Over Delhi Metro Closures Amid Protests
excerpt: Chief Justice warns of judicial action if Supreme Court metro station is not reopened by afternoon, as 16 stations remain shut for the second time this week during student-led protests against exam paper leaks.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • CJI Surya Kant may intervene if the Supreme Court metro station isn't reopened by lunchtime.
  • Delhi Metro closed 16 stations again due to protests, affecting access for lawyers and court staff.
  • PM Modi announced fast-track courts for exam paper leak cases, but protesters demand Education Minister's resignation.
  • Protests against exam paper leaks have entered their 25th day, with over 10,000 participants in recent demonstrations.

Chief Justice of India Surya Kant threatened judicial intervention on Thursday after the closure of 16 Delhi Metro stations — including the one serving the Supreme Court — left lawyers and court staff unable to reach proceedings on time, as student-led protests over exam paper leaks entered their 25th day.

https://x.com/dna/status/2080248369868640304

Supreme Court Bar Association President Vikas Singh raised the issue directly before the CJI, telling the bench that lawyers and Registry staff were stranded because of the shutdowns. Singh proposed that metro passengers with valid Supreme Court entry passes be allowed to exit at the Supreme Court station after security screening, even as other stations remained closed.

"If by lunch time something does not happen to open it, I will intervene."

— CJI Surya Kant

The Chief Justice said the court administration had already taken up the matter with Delhi Metro authorities. He added that judges had been directed not to pass adverse orders against lawyers who could not appear due to logistical difficulties caused by the protests.

Sixteen Stations Shut Across Central Delhi

The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation announced the closure of 16 stations on Thursday morning, the second large-scale shutdown this week, according to Reuters. The affected stations included Lok Kalyan Marg, Rajiv Chowk, Patel Chowk, Ramakrishna Ashram Marg, Barakhamba Road, Supreme Court, Seva Teerth, Janpath, Mandi House, Central Secretariat, ITO, Delhi Gate, Indraprastha, Khan Market, Jor Bagh, and Shivaji Stadium. Interchange facilities remained available at Rajiv Chowk, Mandi House, and Central Secretariat, allowing commuters to switch lines but not enter or exit.

The closures followed fresh violence late Wednesday night. An Assistant Commissioner of Police, Vivek Bhagat, was injured near Tolstoy Marg in the Connaught Place area when a group allegedly attacked security personnel with stones and bottles around 8:30 p.m., according to Delhi Police.

![Delhi Metro. Delhi Metro closed 16 stations again due to protests, affecting access for lawyers and court staff.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/DelhiMetroYellowLine.JPG/3840px-DelhiMetroYellowLine.JPG)

Modi Announces Fast-Track Courts

Hours before the metro shutdowns, Prime Minister Narendra Modi made his first public response to the protests, announcing that fast-track courts would be established to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks. "Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!" Modi posted on X. "Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared."

The Cockroach Janta Party, which launched the protests last month against NEET-UG paper leaks that affected roughly 2 million students, responded by quoting Modi's post with a single demand: "Dharmendra Pradhan Must Resign." Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also dismissed the announcement, accusing Modi of allowing "the total capture and destruction of our education system."

"It has been 25 days so far. Even if it takes 25 months, that is acceptable, but we will not move from here."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder

A Growing Challenge for Modi

What began as an online satire movement has grown into what Reuters described as "the biggest youth challenge to Modi since he came to power in 2014." Over 10,000 people gathered at the Jantar Mantar protest site on Wednesday night, according to local media reports, despite monsoon rains.

The government held one round of talks with CJP leaders earlier this week and offered to debate the issues in parliament. But CJP founder Dipke rejected further negotiations away from the protest site. "If the government wants to talk, it has to come here now," he said.

The protests have also spread beyond Delhi, with demonstrations reported in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Goa, Guwahati, Thiruvananthapuram, Jammu, and Ahmedabad. Opposition parties, including Congress, have seized on the movement, with Gandhi leading protests outside Modi's residence and the Parliament building before being detained on Tuesday.

What to Watch

The CJI's lunchtime deadline marks the first direct collision between the judiciary and the executive fallout from the protests. Whether the Supreme Court metro station reopens — and whether the CJI follows through on his threat of judicial intervention — could set a precedent for the court's role in managing protest-related disruptions to essential services. Meanwhile, the Modi government faces mounting pressure from both the streets and the opposition benches as parliament's monsoon session continues.

nri_angle: The metro closures and escalating protests highlight the deepening dysfunction in India's competitive exam system, an issue of direct concern to diaspora families whose children often pursue Indian university admissions or professional credentials.
